title: Zechariah 8:18–23
context: The LORD finally answers the question about fasting: the fasts of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months will become joyful feasts for Judah, and the people are to love truth and peace. Many peoples will come to seek the LORD in Jerusalem, and ten men from every language will take hold of the skirt of a Jew, saying that they have heard God is with him. The promise is related to Isaiah 2:2–3 and Micah 4:1–2. Readers in both traditions apply it in various ways, including the spread of the gospel among the nations and a future gathering. Shared ground: restoration turns mourning to joy, and God’s presence with his people draws the nations.

verses.text: The word of the LORD of Armies came to me.
verses.arminianNotes:
The word of the LORD of Armies comes to Zechariah. The final sayings of the chapter begin.

Arminian readers see God returning, at last, to the delegation’s question about fasting and answering it with joy.
verses.reformedNotes:
This section answers the question of 7:3 directly.

Reformed readers see God’s word completing the answer begun in chapter 7. Shared ground: both traditions read these closing sayings as the climax of the response to the people’s inquiry about worship.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies says: “The fasts of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months shall be for the house of Judah joy, gladness, and cheerful feasts. Therefore love truth and peace.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The fasts of the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months will become “joy, gladness, and cheerful feasts” for Judah. “Therefore love truth and peace.”

Arminian readers see mourning turned to celebration.
verses.reformedNotes:
The fourth and tenth months are commonly linked with the breach of Jerusalem and the start of the siege (2 Kings 25:1, 3–4; Jeremiah 39:1–2).

Reformed readers agree. Shared ground: restoration turns fasts into feasts.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies says: “Many peoples and the inhabitants of many cities will yet come.
verses.arminianNotes:
Many peoples and inhabitants of many cities will yet come. The nations are drawn in.

Arminian readers see God’s blessing reaching beyond Judah to all who will come.
verses.reformedNotes:
The promise widens the scope of restoration beyond the returned community.

Reformed readers see God’s purpose for the nations. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God’s intention to draw many peoples to himself, as promised elsewhere in the prophets.

verses.text: The inhabitants of one will go to another, saying, ‘Let’s go speedily to entreat the favor of the LORD, and to seek the LORD of Armies. I will go also.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The inhabitants of one city will go to another, saying, “Let’s go speedily to entreat the favor of the LORD,” and “I will go also.” The movement spreads.

Arminian readers see willing response.
verses.reformedNotes:
The invitation of city to city recalls Isaiah 2:3 and Micah 4:2, where many say, “Come, let’s go up to the mountain of the LORD.”

Reformed readers see God drawing the nations. Shared ground: the nations seek the LORD.

verses.text: Yes, many peoples and strong nations will come to seek the LORD of Armies in Jerusalem and to entreat the favor of the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Many peoples and strong nations will come to seek the LORD of Armies in Jerusalem and entreat his favor. The promise is repeated.

Arminian readers see the nations freely turning to God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Readers apply the promise differently: to the spread of the gospel, to a future gathering, or to both. These views are found within both traditions.

Reformed readers see God’s purpose for the nations. Shared ground: the nations will seek the LORD.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies says: “In those days, ten men out of all the languages of the nations will take hold of the skirt of him who is a Jew, saying, ‘We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Ten men from every language will “take hold of the skirt of him who is a Jew,” saying, “We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.”

Arminian readers see the nations drawn by God’s presence.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Ten” may picture a large number.

Reformed readers see God’s presence as the attraction. Fulfillment readings vary within both traditions. Shared ground: God’s presence with his people draws others.
